Mr. Speaker, my first desire is to join with those others who have expressed to you their congratulations upon being elevated to the position of first commoner in this dominion. My pleasure at your appoihtment is enhanced by my recollection of the gallant service you rendered with the Canadian expeditionary force in the first world war.
Today I wish to offer a few comments on the paragraphs in the speech from the throne dealing with national defence. I am sure hon. members of this house and indeed everyone in this dominion will realize with profound regret that it was necessary for a grave warning to be given in the speech from the throne that the hopes for peace and security held out some four years ago have not yet been realized, and that the menace of communism remains with us. However, there will be some measure of reassurance in the promise that this government will pay special attention to the development of research, and that it is the intention of the government to provide the forces with the most modern equipment suitable for present requirements. Members of this party have always endeavoured to adopt a realistic point

The Address-Mr. Pearkes of view on this question of national defence, and I can assure the government that we shall support every effort that is made to supply the forces with that modern equipment the possession of which is so essential to the fulfilment of their great tasks.
Our needs in connection with defence, both as a separate nation and as a signatory to the North Atlantic treaty, have been called to the attention of the house. There is also reference in the speech from the throne to the unification of the services that has taken place already. Rather glowing terms have been used to describe the progress that has been made in this respect. It is a step in the right direction, but so far only the first step has been taken. Old prejudices die hard; and while unification is taking place in regard to the young entries into the services at such points as Royal Roads and Royal Military college, still there is room for much further development along these lines. There has been some unification among the administrative services; yet in the higher ranks, in the realm of command and in organization, we still have three distinct services.
Events which have transpired since the speech from the throne was read have emphasized, if anything, the importance of national defence at the present time. I refer, of course, to the meeting of the North Atlantic council at which representatives of Canada were present, and also to the statement in this house last week by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in connection with the announcement by the President of the United States that an atomic explosion had taken place in the U.S.S.R. It would be interesting to learn whether any of the scientific instruments in our observatories and other scientific centres across the land were able to pick up any echoes of that explosion. I do not think it is beyond the realm of possibility that some of those faint earth tremors recorded last summer may in fact have been the actual results of the explosion which took place in Russia. We have no indication of the date of that explosion, but it is hardly likely that it was a very recent occurrence. There is no reason why scientific instruments could not be developed, if indeed they have not been developed already, which would be able to detect such explosions.
As far as the North Atlantic council is concerned, there is no doubt that soon they will be able to determine the roles the various member nations must play within the broad framework of the defence pattern they are drawing up. According to that pattern it would seem that our contribution might consist in the provision of a strong anti-sub-

marine fleet on both oceans; a limited number of fighter and transport squadrons of the R.C.A.F.; and the maintenance of an airborne brigade of our active army, backed up by a limited number, perhaps four or five divisions, of the reserve army.
As I mentioned, there is a reference in the speech from the throne to the defence needs of Canada as a separate nation. The changes which have taken place within the last few years in the realm of national defence have made it quite clear that, in the event of a third world war, Canada might become a theatre of operations. In recent months considerable attention has been paid to the northern approaches to our country. We have heard descriptions of the extended network of radio and wireless stations which have been established in co-operation with the United States along our northern frontiers.
During the latter months of this summer Exercise Eagle was carried out in the northwest part of our country. This provided an opportunity to study counter-attack methods which might be employed if an enemy made a lodgement on one of our airfields in that part of our territory. In the far west there is a scattered chain of airfields which link Alaska with Canada. The great airfield at Whitehorse is by far the most important link in that chain. The distance from Whitehorse to the Pacific ocean, from which aircraft might be launched from some carrier or even from the fringes of Siberia, is not very much greater than the distance between that airfield and the city of Vancouver or the city of Winnipeg. The distance can be flown within a comparatively few hours.
Exercise Eagle was carried out with a very realistic background. It is possible for an enemy to land airborne troops in that great airfield of Whitehorse if it is not defended. So far as I know there is no ground defence for that airfield today. It is available to any aircraft that may arrive at Whitehorse. During the war it was considered desirable to establish special air defence units consisting of a small highly trained group of men who would be capable of dealing with any parachutists arriving at that field. There were anti-aircraft guns which would have acted as a deterrent to hostile aircraft that might be tempted to land. No such provision is made today. There are no anti-aircraft guns or airdrome defence units at Whitehorse. In this case an ounce of prevention would be worth a pound of cure, as the old adage says.
The country was shocked by the reports which were published by experienced war correspondents who had witnessed Exercise Eagle. They described how the attacking

force was able to hold off the counter-attacking troops, known as Can. Force, which were supposed to represent our troops sent to restore the situation. I do not become unduly alarmed because an exercise discloses certain weaknesses. These exercises have always been so arranged that lessons may be drawn from them. These experiences show whether the equipment provided is adequate, or the training of the troops is such as will meet the particular situation depicted in the narrative leading up to the exercise. There would be no point in having these exercises if there were no lessons to be drawn from them.
As I say, the country has been disturbed by these reports. I hope the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) will take the first opportunity of reassuring this house and the country that any errors which were disclosed or deficiencies which were noticed are being corrected and will not be continued in the future. In particular, I would ask him to assure us that the training of the whole airborne brigade will now be accelerated. This was the first battalion exercise carried out by the one battalion of that brigade which has had any serious training in airborne tactics. Will he give assurance also that the shortages in equipment which were reported, the shortage of parachutes, the shortage of jumping suits are being remedied? Will he assure us also that the right type of aircraft is now being provided both for the fighter squadrons that might accompany such a counter-attacking expedition as was visualized in this exercise and for the transport equipment with the special provisions required for efficient parachute jumping?
There is the additional question of radar sets. I was pleased to note in a report tabled by Canadian Arsenals Limited the other day that developments are taking place in the No. 268 marine set. I hope a similar adaptation is being made so that that set or some other set may co-operate with these mobile forces upon which Canada will depend so much should a raid be made upon our northern frontiers. I come from the Pacific coast, and I may say that we are anxious about the western approaches to our dominion.
Many of the forts which have been established to protect our harbours now have their guns dismantled. The old fifth British Columbia coast regiment of artillery has been changed into a heavy anti-aircraft regiment. I believe that consideration is being given to the reorganization of that regiment. I hope that reorganization will be proceeded
The Address-Mr. Pearkes with so that there will be personnel from the reserve army available to man those forts should they be needed again. Our aerodromes and airfields are few and far between, having regard to the extent of our territory. We are anxious about those approaches. Those approaches must be watched. I think it is therefore high time that a special plea should be put in now for the stationing on the Pacific coast of the second aircraft carrier, a sister ship to H.M.C.S. Magnificent, which is stationed mainly on the Atlantic seaboard. Such a vessel would be able to co-operate with the anti-aircraft school of artillery located at Esquimalt. It may be comparatively easy to borrow a submarine, but it will not be so easy at a moment's notice to borrow an aircraft carrier.
This summer I had the opportunity of inspecting one of the United States coastguard cutters which was visiting our harbour of Nanaimo. Those United States ships are used mainly for watching the approaches. They are stationed from five hundred miles to one thousand miles out in the Pacific off the coast of Oregon but a gap exists between those ships stationed off the coast of Oregon and the Aleutian islands in the north. The vessel I inspected was a magnificent one, fully equipped with the latest radar and radio apparatus. One of its functions in peacetime is to plot the route of all aircraft passing within range of its instruments. By that method it was able to report, to an aircraft which might have lost its direction, its exact location. It had the means of assisting in air rescue work at sea. Amidships of that vessel was a huge compartment in which the weather balloons could be blown up and from which they could be released, enabling reports to be made upon weather conditions in the Pacific. Those meteorological reports of course have great value in peace or in war. I say a gap exists between those watchers of the approaches from the Pacific off the Oregon coast and the Aleutian islands. The time has come when we can no longer depend solely upon the United States, not only to provide the information which they send in with regard to the weather and planes which pass over them, but also for the services they continually render in saving lives and saving our ships at sea.
In this gap there is also a shortage of aircraft to report upon the approach lines. It is beyond my comprehension why there are such great delays in authorizing the auxiliary squadron of the R.C.A.F. at Victoria. For years now, representations have been made from the southern portion of Vancouver island from young men of the finest possible type who wish to serve voluntarily in such

The Address-Mr. Pearkes an auxiliary squadron. Years are going by and these men are beginning to lose heart. They are wondering whether a squadron will ever be authorized.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned for the dinner recess I was speaking about the lack of support which had been given to the formation of the auxiliary R.C.A.F. squadron at Victoria. These auxiliary or reserve units were in previous years the medium by which the miracle was worked whereby great masses of citizens from Canada were welded into military formations and were able to make so grand a contribution to the successful conduct of the first and second world wars.
It was the willingness of innumerable Canadian citizens to give up their spare time, their holidays, and their evenings in order to learn voluntarily the rudiments of military science, and something by way of a smattering of the art of leadership, that enabled them in the hour of crisis to develop those great masses of Canadian citizens who came forward into, as I said a moment ago, a really effective fighting force.
I feel the time still continues when every possible encouragement should be given to our non-permanent sailors, soldiers and airmen; and I regret it has not been possible for the government to encourage those young men from the southern part of Vancouver island, who are anxious to continue their service in the auxiliary arm of the R.C.A.F.
The government has given greater encouragement to the reserve army units than was ever given before. I say it is imperative upon the government to see that the policies which they have enunciated regarding the effective training of the officers and non-commissioned officers of those units are carried out to the letter. Before the last war, and for a number of years, the non-permanent units of this country were kept alive through the work done by the corps of officers and non-commissioned officers in those units. It is important that every encouragement be given to them to train along up-to-date lines. 1 believe encouragement is being given, but in some cases there is a tendency to emphasize the importance of recruiting, administration and keeping alive the traditions of the various units rather than going ahead with effective and up-to-date training.
In connection with the anxiety felt on the Pacific coast regarding the state of our defences there, as may be felt in other parts of the country as well, it was only a couple

of years ago that Major General Worthington was appointed director and organizer of the civil defence of this country. If, as I claimed earlier in my remarks, Canada is in a position where it might become an active theatre of war, if war broke out again, then the importance of civil defence is such as has never been experienced in this land before. Some two years have elapsed since that appointment was made. I hope the minister will be able to tell us what progress has been made along these lines.
I have heard some talk about the importance of standardizing fire-fighting equipment. Unfortunately the fire departments of the various cities find their equipment is not co-ordinated. The result is that frequently when a fire occurs the fire brigades from neighbouring towns are unable to assist because their hose reels are not of the same standard or same make or size as those in the town where the fire has occurred. That is one direction in which it is imperative that some action be taken.
Also I would suggest that, in so far as the training of medical service is concerned, thought might be given to the type of casualties and injuries which might occur should this country be subjected to some modern form of attack.
I believe that in the majority of reserve units recruiting is going reasonably well. I would put forward one suggestion, however, namely that as a result of the extension of the franchise at the last general election many new groups of Canadians have now been brought within the realm of full Canadian citizenship. I feel those new groups should be encouraged to assume their responsibilities in every branch of citizenship.
On the Pacific coast we have thousands of young men of East Indian origin, their forebears having come from India, or from what is now called Pakistan. They come from martial races. These young men, born in Canada, have inherited those qualities of loyalty and courage which were so marked among the Hindus and Sikhs in the various units of the Indian and British armies. I hope a definite effort will be made to encourage these new Canadians to join with our defence forces. I know of no means whereby communism among the ranks of those men could better be combated than by having them assume the full responsibility of citizenship.
Only a few days ago I was advised that the Royal Humane Society in Canada had seen fit to recognize a young Hindu boy who had been responsible for saving the lives of two other boys in lake Cowichan. He is the son of Bal Singh, an East Indian resident of

Vancouver island, who served during the first world war, and is now an active member of our branch of the Legion.
I mention that only to show that these Canadian-born East Indians have inherited the qualities of courage and valour and loyalty which made their sires so famous in the annals of the military history of the British empire.
In closing, I should like to say one word with regard to the veterans of this land, the old soldiers. Since the opening of the session we have heard that the pound has been devalued. I was pleased to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) say that those veterans who are drawing an imperial pension, and at the same time have that pension brought up to Canadian standards by a supplementary Canadian pension, will have that supplementary pension increased so that they will not suffer from the devaluation of the pound.
Of course there are still hundreds, perhaps thousands, of imperial ex-servicemen in this land who are not qualified for that supplementary Canadian pension. If they are drawing a pension from the British ministry of pensions, that pension is pitifully small now. I believe I am correct in saying that a widow's pension is 45 shillings a week, which, before devaluation of the pound, would have been somewhere in the neighbourhood of $9 a week. Now it is less than $7. It is pretty hard for a hundred per cent disabled pensioner, or the widow of a service man, to exist with a reasonable standard of living on that small pension. I do hope that something will be worked out, either by an extension of the War Veterans Allowance Act or by agreement between this government and the government of Great Britain, whereby our comrades who served with forces other than Canadian forces will be able to maintain themselves and their families in a position which is not infinitely inferior to that in which this government permits Canadian exservicemen to maintain themselves. Of course I am referring only to those veterans of the imperial forces who have lived for a long period in this country.

May I be allowed at this point to raise a question which I would have preferred to bring up in the absence of the Prime Minister, but which I wish nevertheless to discuss. If heretofore, because of special circumstances, an official residence for the Prime Minister was considered unessential, surely the situation is now such that this lack should be remedied without further delay.
When Canada receives distinguished visitors, the Prime Minister as such has no home in which to welcome them, while ambassadors have all they need to honour not only foreign visitors but Canadians also. Abroad, in every capital city of the world, Canada is in an excellent position to entertain these guests. We should therefore provide our first citizen and his distinguished lady with what is needed to enhance the prestige of the name Canada and of the Canadian capital.	It
would, of course, be easy to appeal to the generosity of the public; I have no doubt that the funds required for the purchase of a suitable residence would immediately be

The Address-Mr. Lesage forthcoming. I feel, however, that every Canadian should participate in the offer of a house which our Prime Minister would occupy in his official capacity, and which would then be at the disposal of all future Canadian prime ministers.
As we shall see, Canada is well on the way to self-government. National pride therefore makes it imperative that we provide the Prime Minister and his wife with an official home where, henceforward, they may entertain important guests.
With the hearty commendation of the house, I therefore beg the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to include without further delay, in the supplementary estimates that will be brought down this autumn, the sum required for the purpose I have just outlined.
Mr. Speaker, extremely interesting proposals, from the constitutional and legal viewpoints, are to be found in the speech from the throne. Last Friday, those proposals were explained from a constitutional point of view by the Prime Minister in the following words, and I quote from page 197 of Hansard:
From time to time modifications have been made in provincial constitutions by those who had the authority and were concerned about them, and no one else was consulted or had to be consulted. What is forecast in the speech from the throne Is that there will be an application to the parliament at Westminster to say that such amendments to the Canadian constitution as do not affect the jurisdiction of the provinces, or the rights or privileges secured to the provinces, or the minority rights I referred to previously, can be made here in this parliament instead of being made in the parliament at Westminster on motions or addresses adopted by this parliament. That is the only purpose and effect of the measure forecast in the speech from the throne. But that measure would leave to the courts the responsibility and the burden of deciding what is within provincial jurisdiction or constitutes a provincial right and what is of concern only to the federal authority and their decisions will be binding as they have been in the past.
The right hon. the Prime Minister mentioned in his speech that since confederation, on ten separate occasions, addresses have been forwarded to the parliament in London by this parliament, with a view to amending our constitution. Never did the parliament at Westminster refuse to accept these addresses and to amend the Canadian constitution. Yet the provinces were never consulted in any one of these cases and the British parliament simply approved the proposed amendments in the manner of a formality. Experience has shown that it will refuse none of this parliament's requests for amendments to the constitution. Who would dare suggest that this can change now?

This situation has come about in practice as Canada acquires in the world an ever-increasing importance, not only in the economic field, but on the international scene. That is why, as a matter of fact, the Prime Minister, a year or two ago, expressed the fear that the parliament at Westminster could, in the manner of a formality, approve an address from this parliament requesting, for instance-that is the example he chose- that section 133 of the British North America Act be abolished.
In practice, the present position is that the federal parliament, I repeat, may ask for and obtain any amendment whatsoever to the constitution. But the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, suggests that we, ourselves, limit the powers granted the Canadian parliament through constant practice. In fact, this approval by the British parliament has become a mere formality. The Prime Minister has suggested that in the future the law should take precedence over practice and absolutely guarantee the rights of the provinces and of the minorities. The law would state that the federal government shall be free to amend the constitution within the realm of its exclusive jurisdiction and that each of the provinces is free within the realm of its exclusive jurisdiction. But the federal government may not now amend the constitution in matters pertaining to the rights of minorities and the rights of the provinces, in matters concerning only the provinces or in questions of mixed jurisdiction.
Thus, for instance, the field of direct taxation is a field of mixed jurisdiction where both the central authority and the provincial legislatures can operate. The prime minister of the province of Quebec expressed certain fears on that subject. Now, Mr. Speaker, parliament will not be able to amend the constitution with respect to that field, and Mr. Duplessis will certainly have the chance to discuss the question and to assert the needs of the provinces at the conference he has been invited to attend by the Prime Minister of Canada, in order precisely to come to an understanding on the possible means of amending the constitution, in a way satisfactory to all parties, in fields of mixed jurisdiction, such as direct taxation.
Therefore, the law will henceforth tell the parliament at Ottawa that it can amend the constitution only in matters coming under its sole jurisdiction. And as that will be written into our statutes, the party that deems itself injured will be able to appeal to the tribunals, whereas up to now a province which believed its rights had been encroached upon could

not appeal to the tribunals as long as the proposed amendments had been ratified by the British parliament. Thus the provinces gain an additional right. -
All things considered, far from being an encroachment upon provincial and minority rights, such a reform constitutes a further double guarantee, based on law and justice. Indeed, the written law will replace a constitutional practice fraught with danger for the minorities and the provinces. Efficient legal remedy will be afforded to minorities and provinces if they believe that their rights have been infringed upon.
It is perhaps on account of that new remedy that most objections have been and are still voiced against the abolition of appeals to the privy council. Last year, during the discussion on a bill introduced by Mr. Jaenicke, I went fully into that matter. I maintained that the privy council was a political court, that its members were politicians and that they had not the independence which our supreme court judges enjoy. I claimed that the members of the privy council are not familiar with our customs and that, in the last analysis, the members of the supreme court are more qualified to mete out justice and equity to Canadians than are the members of a court which sits outside this country. I also went at length into the jurisprudence of the supreme court and the privy council on constitutional cases, and I came to the conclusion that past experience proves, beyond any doubt, that the supreme court affords more safeguards than the privy council as regards the protection of minorities and the defence of provincial rights.
Moreover, let us not forget that, through the bill which is now before the house, the supreme court will now be composed of nine judges, three of which will be from the province of Quebec. That constitutes an extremely important additional guarantee for the rights of minorities. But after all what counts most is that, thanks be to God, my country's courts are second to none, as far as the judges' integrity is concerned. Breaches against justice, and when I say justice I mean justice, have perhaps brought many Canadian citizens to believe that such a virtue tends to disappear. Claims held in totalitarian countries to the effect that might is right have perhaps shaken faith in justice. But I can assure my fellow citizens that our magistrates have that virtue of justice engraved in their hearts and wish to give everyone his due, whether individuals, corporations, municipalities, provinces or central government are concerned. They are fully aware of their responsibility in the
The Address-Mr. Lesage accomplishment of the most important function the state has delegated to them as one of its foremost prerogatives.
According to Aristotle, the prince is the keeper of justice. Justice is an outgrowth of the essential attribute of the state. It is one of the three functions, of the three powers of a sovereign country, namely the executive, the legislative and the judicial powers. We shall not be autonomous so long as we are unable to amend our own constitution. We are not in full possession of our legislative powers and we do not enjoy complete judicial independence. We only enjoy one power, the executive power, and this on account of the legal friction pertaining to the divisibility of the crown. We do not enjoy the two other powers, namely full legislative and judicial powers. Mr. Speaker, over twenty years ago, when I was only sixteen, I took part in my first public debate, together with my good friend, who is now my colleague, the member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pinard). We did not consult each other, because I was in Quebec and he was in Montreal, but we both discussed the following subject: "Canada among nations". Both of us, without consulting each other, claimed for Canada all the attributes of sovereignty. That was prior to 1931, before the enactment of the Statute of Westminster.
At the time, we may have been looked upon as dreamers. I am not sure whether this speech I had written when so young had inspired me with a particular feeling of national pride or not, but later on, whenever I addressed the public, I felt it my duty to claim the attributes of sovereignty for my country. At every step Canada took towards autonomy, whether in the international or in the national field, I felt deeply moved, my patriotism fired me with enthusiasm. When I heard the Prime Minister outline his constitutional platform over the radio, which has been stated in the speech from the throne, I was deeply moved and proud of my country, after the years I had spent claiming its autonomy, after I had asked my electors for a mandate in order that I may claim here my country's sovereignty. I was indeed very happy.
When the Prime Minister outlined his program to my electors at Montmagny, on May 22 last, I was proud to be a Canadian and a fellow citizen of our leader. That is why I asked my constituents to give him an unequivocal mandate.
He obtained that unequivocal mandate not only from the electors of Montmagny-L'Islet, not only from the whole of the province of

The Address-Mr. Lesage Quebec, but from the constituents of nearly every electoral district throughout Canada. It is therefore with an unequivocal mandate that he now comes before parliament to ask both houses for their approval of the program which has already been sanctioned by the people who sent us here when they voted for us last June.
Some people would like to see these measures postponed. No good ever comes of delaying too long, Mr. Speaker. In the past, important problems were submitted to a dominion-provincial conference. Without censuring anyone, I point out that unfortunately certain interests availed themselves of that occasion to boost their political capital and gain the confidence of the electors. Why did that happen? Because the subject under consideration at those conferences was so broad that the delegates could go off at a tangent. On the other hand, we have held many dominion-provincial conferences quietly, smoothly and without fanfare, at which federal and provincial authorities were in agreement. For that reason, I feel that in recommending that the debate on amendments to the constitution be restricted to problems involving joint jurisdiction or relating to minorities, the Prime Minister has made an excellent proposal.
I fail to see why we should require the assent of the provinces when dealing with matters that concern only the dominion any more than they would need the concurrence of the federal parliament in spheres entirely under their control.
If a federal-provincial conference is being planned to deal with so broad a matter, I feel sure that, after our experience of the past, it will lead to no practical results. Inevitably, passions will be aroused, the issue will be dodged and this, finally, can only lead to the failure of such a conference, whereas by concentrating on a given question, the Prime Minister has already laid the groundwork of an almost certain success. After all, a spirit of co-operation, of tolerance and of justice, is all that can be required of those attending such a conference.
I would not want anyone and especially those who represent the minority, of which I am a part, to concede a single one of the rights guaranteed by the letter of confederation and which are today, I insist, threatened because of a constitutional practice which has forced itself upon us since 1837. Not for any consideration would I want one single shred of minority or provincial rights to be transferred to this parliament. I am confident that the autonomy of the provinces will be

safeguarded, but I also hope that, in order to ensure Canada's continued growth, those fields which were given to the federal government by the fathers of confederation will also be protected. After all, if the provinces are entitled to their autonomy, we are also entitled to ours. The parliament of Canada must be free to act in those fields which are its sote responsibility and on no account should those who represent the central authorities be willing to abandon even one single shred of its rights. But each delegate, while prepared to defend the rights of those whom he represents, should come to this conference in a spirit of tolerance, co-operation and Canadian patriotism. Thus, we may be sure that this conference will meet with success.
If agreement is reached on the manner in which our constitution can be amended in all fields, only one additional step will be required to make it truly Canadian, one to be written in the statutes of this parliament and in those of the various provinces of Canada. Then we shall have achieved complete sovereignty, a dream that has been with us for so long.

Mr. T. G. W. Ashbourne (Grand Falls-White
Bay): Mr. Speaker, I should like my first remarks in this house to be words of thanks to the electors of the riding of Grand Falls-White Bay in Newfoundland, which riding consists of the electoral districts of Grand Falls, Green Bay, White Bay and Labrador, the last named including an area of some
113,000	square miles. I want to thank the electors for the confidence they have expressed in sending me to this historic House of Commons, and I am very happy to be here.
To you, sir, I should like to add my congratulations to those already expressed by other hon. members on your election as Speaker of this house. There is an air of permanence about this august chamber. I trust that you will long be spared to fulfil the duties of your exalted position which, I hope, will prove a delight to you and of benefit to us. I am delighted to congratulate our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the leader of the great Liberal party, on the success of our party in the election of June 27. His outstanding qualities of leadership played an important role in the magnitude of this great victory.
I should like to offer my congratulations also to the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) on the excellent

speeches they delivered as mover and seconder of the motion which is now under discussion. As yet it has not been my privilege to visit Vancouver, but after listening with rapt attention to the address of the member for Vancouver South, I feel that, as soon as I can conveniently do so, I should like to visit that part of Canada.
The visit of His Excellency the Governor General and Viscountess Alexander to Newfoundland was greatly appreciated by our people. This visit afforded many of them an opportunity of meeting the representative of His Majesty the King, whose health we trust will continue to improve. I sincerely hope that the welcome accorded to the governor general, and the repeated desire expressed by the people of Newfoundland for a return visit by His Excellency and his good lady, will promote an early return so that the places not yet visited by them may have an opportunity of greeting them.
We were honoured by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who, practically speaking, ended his election campaign tour in Newfoundland. I feel sure that the remembrance of the deep interest displayed by the right hon. gentleman in the province of Newfoundland, and his constant efforts to bring the union of Newfoundland and Canada to a satisfactory consummation, was in the minds of the people of Canada.
Since I had the honour of being elected by the people of Newfoundland to be a member of the national convention which met in St. John's on September 11, 1946, I can speak with a certain degree of personal knowledge about the work of that convention. It happens that I was also a member of the delegation elected by the national convention to come to Ottawa in the summer of 1947 to confer with representatives of the Canadian government about the possible terms of union. I want to pay tribute to the ex-Prime Minister, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, who welcomed us at that time, as well as to the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent, who acted as chairman of the meetings that were held at that time.
We arrived in this city on the 24th day of June, the day on which the people of Newfoundland were celebrating the four hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the landing of John Cabot upon the shores of that province. The delegation remained here for a period of three months, during which time meetings were held, concluding on September 29, 1947. One month from that day the Prime Minister of Canada wrote to His Excellency Sir Gordon, now Lord Macdonald, the Governor
The Address-Mr. Ashbourne of Newfoundland, enclosing a statement of terms believed to constitute a fair and equitable basis for union with Canada. Those terms were discussed at length by the members of the national convention and were before the people in the referenda which followed.
The national convention had been elected by the people of Newfoundland to examine the financial and economic condition of the country and to make recommendations to the British government as to the forms of government to be submitted to the people in a national referendum. The first referendum was held on June 3, 1948, the results of which are as follows: for continuation of commission of government for a five-year period, 22,311; for confederation with Canada, 64,066; for restoration of responsible government, 69,400. As no form of government had received a majority of the votes cast, a second referendum was held on July 22, 1948. This resulted in confederation with Canada receiving 78,323 votes as against 71,334 votes for responsible government.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. F. G. Bradley, the Secretary of State for Canada, was the chairman of the delegation that came to Ottawa in the summer of 1947. When we returned to the convention in Newfoundland both of us, in common with fourteen other members of the convention, felt that the people of Newfoundland should be afforded an opportunity of voting upon the matter of confederation with Canada. I can assure you we were very glad when the British government decided to place it upon the ballot paper. Confederation, I am happy to say, is now a fait accompli. On the 15th day of September, 1949, when this twenty-first parliament assembled, we saw the representatives of Newfoundland seated in this chamber with the representatives of the other nine provinces.
We are proud and happy to take our places in this great land, and delighted that at long last the representations, discussions, conferences and negotiations have borne fruit. As a result of the choice of the people, on whose judgment we can safely rely, I am happy that we are now part and parcel of this great dominion which is, if I may be allowed to say so, greater now that the resources of Newfoundland have been pooled with those of Canada. We can appreciate the fact that the majority of the people are never far wrong when their voice can be heard or when an opportunity is given them to express their considered will on issues concerning their future and their welfare. As time goes on, and as the needs of Newfoundland become
258	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Ashbourne more apparent, I have faith and confidence that from the people of Canada, and from their representatives in this parliament and other assemblies, we shall receive the utmost consideration commensurate with the ability of this dominion to satisfy the needs of Newfoundland as they may arise.
I wish to voice my warm appreciation of the words of welcome contained in the speech from the throne with regard to the advent of Newfoundlanders in this parliament, and to place on record my own high regard for that spirit of friendliness, harmony and good will so pleasantly manifested since the beginning of this session. We in Newfoundland have not been unaccustomed to the storms which have swept our province as well as other provinces represented here. We have felt the tremor of the earthquake. We have been shaken, as it were, by convulsions. Yet, undaunted, we have carried on as well as we could. When the great depressions struck our economic structure we were unfortunately not able, unaided, to carry on alone. For a time we were governed by the commission of government, which I believe did a good job as a whole in Newfoundland. But it was not a democratic form of government; while at the time it seemed to be a good expedient, it was only to be expected that the people of Newfoundland would want responsible government. Today we have responsible government, not on our own but backed up with the resources of the great Dominion of Canada.
Newfoundland is a country of proverbial beauty. We have our majestic headlands, some of them rising in sheer grandeur hundreds of feet, and down the steep slopes come tumbling the waterfalls. I have not yet had the privilege of viewing the Grand Falls of Labrador. I have not yet visited Labrador although I have the honour to represent that great area. But it will be my duty and privilege some day to visit that great country. We know something of the tremendous assets to be found in Labrador, of the rich mines and of the virgin forests which are hers. In imagination we look back to the sight which must have met the eyes of John Cabot when, on the far-away day, coming to the shores of Newfoundland, he and his fellow voyageurs exclaimed, "Buena vista!" I may say that the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley) resides in Bonavista and represents that historic district as well as the district of Twillingate.
I believe there is a widespread belief that Newfoundland is a land of fogs and ice, but that is not correct. Because of the Arctic current, which flows from the north down
[Mr, Ashbourne.)

toward the gulf stream, a certain amount of fog is naturally generated. But I can assure hon. members that the climate of Newfoundland as a whole is exceptionally good. I might say that right here in this House of Commons I should like to feel some of those sea breezes that I have felt in the past. I mention the climate of Newfoundland because I realize what a tremendous asset it is to us. To those people who want to get away from the sweltering heat of the city in the summertime I would extend an invitation to come down and enjoy the climate of Newfoundland. We have our beautiful days of sunshine and nights that are cool, so that one can lie down and have a decent rest. We in Newfoundland realize that in our climate we have an attraction which I hope will bring many tourists to our shores.
We have as well the salmon fishing about which a good many hon. members know. My good friend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) will be able to tell you more about that attraction. I have never yet had the thrill of catching a salmon. Now that I am a member of the House of Commons I do not know whether I shall have the time to go salmon fishing. Up to the present time my life has been so crowded that I have not been able to indulge in that sport. I mention it, however, because there may be some who would like to come down and enjoy the salmon fishing in Newfoundland.
It is true that we have some fog, particularly at certain periods of the year, especially in the spring. Later on I shall be making requisitions to the government for some fog alarms and also for some lighthouses, which are most necessary for the people residing in the districts I have the honour to represent. As they go north in quest of the harvests of the deep, these fishermen are oftentimes impeded by fog in the spring of the year. I feel sure that my request for a certain number of fog alarms and lighthouses will not fall on deaf ears, and that the people of Canada will see that these are provided for our fishermen. We know these men who are seeking to provide food for the people of the world will be helped in their endeavours, and I can assure the house that it will be highly appreciated by them.
Newfoundland's strategic position, being so to speak the Gibraltar of the North American continent, is well known. I am happy that our lot is now cast with the rest of the people of Canada, and that this dominion is now rounded out by the inclusion of Newfoundland. We are primarily a fishing country. The prolific cod fisheries of Newfound-

land have meant bread and butter to our people. We have also our salmon fisheries, our lobster fisheries and our herring fisheries.
I was greatly taken with the desire of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) to give aid to the fishermen. In Newfoundland the fisheries have been our chief mainstay and, as I said before, they offer much by way of food to the people of the world. For example, let us consider the herring fishery. The herring is one of the most important of food fishes, and they are found in our bays and along the Labrador coast. We realize that at the present time, on account of the devaluation of the dollar, if we are to keep up consumption in the export markets we may have to reduce our fish prices. On the other hand we sell a considerable quantity of codfish to Puerto Rico. There we shall receive American dollars which, I trust, will offset some of the loss which may be incurred by the devaluation of other currencies.
In Newfoundland we have an organization called NAFEL. This is the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters, Limited, which organization handles the sales of codfish for the exporters of Newfoundland. We have learned from experience the evils of consigning fish to markets without receiving payment beforehand. We have also learned to our sorrow of the cutthroat competition when, in order to make a sale in a market, one exporter might be inclined to undercut another. I am happy to say we now have NAFEL, which is looking after the exporting of our codfish.
I should like briefly to refer to a few of the matters included in the speech from the throne. In my opinion this was a good speech, forecasting as it did important legislation, some of which has already been placed before the house. It is my hope that the dominion-provincial conference, which in my opinion is a worthy project, may result in profitable progress, and may achieve the desired end, with each participant actively motivated toward a common goal. By that method I am sure the best possible results will flow for the people and the nation.
The right to amend our own constitution should surely be our own prerogative. It seems to me we must continue to strive with determination and in the spirit of cooperation not merely to find temporary solutions for our problems, but adequate and lasting ones, in all the matters which we undertake. I am pleased to see the increasing interest taken in national health, which primarily, I understand, is a provincial matter.
May I say that in my first speech in the house I realize that I have much to learn. I am only a beginner here, and there are 45781-17
The Address-Mr. Ashbourne many directions in which I shall have to make progress slowly. It is not easy to change quickly from one course of procedure to another. The amount of $30 million voted at the last session of parliament to be divided among the provinces was, in my opinion, a proper step. I am afraid, however, Newfoundland may be unable to participate in all the various grants.
For example, I am not sure that we shall be able to take up the amount of money which was voted for cancer research. It would be, I think, a great pity for any amounts that we could not possibly take for the different sections for which the votes were granted to go into a dropped balance. I trust that if there are any such amounts which cannot be used for grants as indicated, they may be credited to Newfoundland, and given to us for certain other medical and health purposes. For instance, I have in mind hospital construction. We have in Newfoundland a health problem. Those grants in toto could be used for various purposes in Newfoundland to which we could profitably put them. We have several cottage hospitals, as well as private hospitals. We have the hospitals in the north operated by the International Grenfell Association, which operates a large hospital at St. Anthony, and also on the coast of Labrador. We have at my home town of Twillingate a memorial hospital built as a memorial to the men in world war I who laid down their lives in that great conflict.
On August 17 last we celebrated the 25th anniversary of the opening of the Notre Dame Memorial hospital. Newfoundland being an island, our main means of transportation is by boat, and in Newfoundland the people are scattered among the various outports around the coasts. I was talking to Dr. Olds, the superintendent of the hospital in Twillingate, just shortly before I left. It might be interesting to note that he is a graduate of the Johns Hopkins university. He has been at Twillingate for quite a period. He is the missionary type of doctor and at one time during the war he practically carried on single-handed at this 130-bed hospital. He was telling me how much he would like to have an aeroplane in order that cases might be brought to the hospital more quickly. We were delighted to hear that the United States government has donated a large sum of money for the building of a hospital at St. Lawrence on the southwest coast of Newfoundland.
We in Newfoundland are looking forward to the building of the trans-Canada highway and we hope that a highway will also be built across Newfoundland and Labrador. We understand that a ferry service across Cabot

The Address-Mr. Ashbourne
strait will be instituted in time and this would permit many people to come from the mainland to visit our beauty spots and enjoy the fishing and hunting available in Newfoundland. There are herds of moose and caribou on the island which are increasing all the time, but I think we shall have to bring in some deer from the mainland, which would add greatly to the attractions of our hunting.
We have heard much said about the premium on gold, but may I suggest that a premium on food would not be out of order. In the final analysis, is not food of greater value than gold? We in Newfoundland have helped to feed the people of the world. Our climate is such that we are able to dry the salt cod which we have exported, not only to the Mediterranean, to the West Indies and to Puerto Rico, but to Brazil.
While we look forward to a further development of the fresh fish industry we realize that there is a great demand for the salted product. I hope and trust that Europe will still be able to take large quantities of our codfish. Unfortunately we have not been able to sell any cod in Spain for two years. There may be a necessary curtailment in our exports of fish owing to lack of currency, but it would be a great thing if we could once more sell our products to Spain. I remember one time being told by a fish merchant there that if we could produce a certain quality of fish it would sell in that market no matter what other cargoes might be offering. This question of exchange has hampered our exports to the extent, as I have stated, that we have not been able to make any sales of fish in Spain for quite some time.
Shipbuilding is mentioned in the speech from the throne. This is a most important industry, a most essential industry to Newfoundland. Being an insular and maritime country we must depend upon shipping. If it is the intention of the government to foster the shipbuilding industry I hope they will also consider the matter of repairs to existing hulls. It is a well-known fact that the bottom of a vessel will outlast two top structures. Not having a great deal of hardwood in Newfoundland, we must use the softer varieties, and we find that the topsides give out first. The bottom of the vessel, being in contact with salt water, is quite often perfectly sound when the upper part must be condemned. If repairs, under supervision of course, could be carried on I know that the fishermen would be delighted and I think provisions for such repair work might well be coupled with the measure proposed.

I wish to thank hon. members of the house for their indulgence. Mining is a great asset to Newfoundland. The mines at Buchans provide considerable employment and we are looking forward to the development of the mineral resources in Labrador.
The production of newsprint at Grand Falls and Corner Brook has been a means of reducing unemployment throughout the island and also of obtaining United States dollars.
Then a word with regard to the air agreements. No doubt the acquisition by Canada of Gander airport, which is in my riding, strengthened the hands of the government in the finalization of these agreements. If further details have not yet been decided upon, or remain to be ironed out, I trust that in the final analysis no undue friction will develop, but that the result will be expanded services and greater employment with a consequent need for additional Newfoundland personnel. The large airport at Gander, the centre of international air travel, the crossroads of the world, will, I believe, play a most important role in the development of our country.
The matter of forest conservation is most essential. Fire, that great menace, has been a constant threat. The change-over from coal to oil burning locomotives in Newfoundland has resulted already in fewer fires. Newfoundland, if denuded of her forests, would become in time a bald rock. Then our fisheries would disappear and storms would likely sweep over her.
I sincerely say "amen" to the prayer that Divine Providence may bless our deliberations on behalf of this great Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, while I intend to be very brief in my remarks, I want to discuss certain matters of particular importance to my constituency, and to Canada as a whole. One of those subjects is irrigation.
Before discussing it may I take this opportunity to congratulate the Speaker of the house and also you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on being elevated to your high offices. May I congratulate the mover (Mr. Boisvert) and the seconder (Mr. Laing) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I regret that I was unable to follow the speech of the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska owing to my meagre knowledge of the French language, but I certainly enjoyed the address of the hon. member for Vancouver South. I think he did a wonderful job, and I am sure that we are going to hear more good speeches from the same hon. member.

Coming over to this side of the house, may I offer my congratulations to another member from the other end of Canada, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins). I enjoyed listening to his speech, and I am sure everyone else did. I believe that he is another hon. member who will certainly be heard from in the future. I am sure that we will take pleasure in the contributions that he will make to the debates of the house.
The subject of irrigation is one that is certainly not new to most hon. members, and it is one that is not new within the walls of this chamber. I hope that the word "irrigation" will ring through this chamber until our wish to see our western plains well supplied with water has been fulfilled. During the past week we have had several celebrations in Lethbridge in connection with irrigation. The Lethbridge chamber of commerce was celebrating their seventy-fifth anniversary, and at the same time they had a celebration in connection with irrigation, a subject in which they have taken an interest ever since they were first organized. They have done a wonderful job in promoting irrigation, not only in the Lethbridge area but also in the Medicine Hat area, and other areas as well.
I might mention in passing that Mr. John Fisher, the noted C.B.C. commentator, covered the celebration last week. I am sure that many hon. members of the house must have heard Mr. Fisher either on Saturday afternoon or yesterday when he gave Canada the story of irrigation, and what irrigation has done for the Lethbridge community. I find that many members of the staff of the house also listened to him. I want to congratulate the Prime Minister upon his great victory on June 27. A small part of that victory brings me to this house to represent the constituency of Moose Mountain as a member of the government party. Much has been said about the results of the general election. I intend to speak for myself and for a good many of my colleagues from Saskatchewan. We out there ran our campaign fairly well on the past policies of the Liberal government. My colleagues and I were elected to this house under the policies of the Department of Agriculture. We in Saskatchewan made few if any promises because we knew that, if we promised the moon, our opposition out there would promise something bigger.
Much has been said about the government's majority in the House of Commons. As a new member I do not know a great deal about majorities or strong oppositions. I do believe however that a large majority is not something which need go amiss, because it gives hon. members supporting the government an opportunity to criticize that government, and to question it freely. Much has been said about housing. I shall not linger long on that subject, but there are some brief observations I should like to make. I believe all hon. members will agree that the housing situation in Canada is not in as satisfactory a condition as we would like to see it. I believe I can speak for a large section of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and for cities in those provinces. True, there is a backlog in housing; but if we were to consider the situation in Winnipeg, which all will agree is a large city in which more than half the population of Manitoba lives, we would find
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith that we could drive down street after street, avenue after avenue and see on each street or avenue new houses, either already completed or in process of being built. I believe we could take a page out of the book of the eastern farmers. We will have to do as they are doing, namely reseed our lands to grass. I am told that right here in the Ottawa valley, where there is great fertility and plenty of rain, the farmers cannot grow crops continually. Occasionally they have to sow their lands to legumes and grasses. Sooner or later we in western Canada have to follow a similar course.
It is true that some farmers in the west are beginning to follow that procedure. However, if we are going to keep our land young we will have to sow grass. Let us keep in mind that people must eat.
Much has been said about decreases in farm prices. Some of those prices have gone down; but the average for the first three months of 1949 showed an all-time high. We are still enjoying prices which are two and a half times higher than in the pre-war period.
It is my belief however that prices are bound to come down. In my view that is essential, because it will be agreed that when prices get too high they are bound to react to a point where they are too low. We know that, under the world wheat agreement, from year to year we are going to take less for our wheat. I do not think there is a wheat grower in Canada who, if he gave the matter serious consideration, would not admit that that is a satisfactory set-up. What we want


is stability. We do not want a high price one time and a low price the next time.

I represent the rural constituency of Kindersley, which contains some of the best grain-growing land in Saskatchewan and probably in all western Canada. It also includes land on which people were settled years ago and which perhaps was the wrong type of land for that purpose. By the policies carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has created community pastures in these areas, and where at one time the people were in serious difficulties in trying to grow wheat, at the present time they are carrying on a profitable cattle industry and the country is being rehabilitated.
The Minister of Agriculture under this same prairie farm assistance has been able to take care of certain people living in areas where it has been impossible to grow grain or raise cattle, and it is to be hoped that in the not too distant future it will be possible to provide in the province land to which these people may be moved where they will be able to be self-supporting and lead happy lives without any economic worries.
Another reason for my speaking on this motion is to correct some impressions. Driving from my constituency of Kindersley to Ottawa, I feel after driving for about three days that I am never going to get here. When I get here I realize that when I am at home I am over a thousand miles from the west coast and when I am here I am still another thousand or more miles from the new

province of Newfoundland, which I wish to welcome at this time. I then realize how impossible it is for the people of this country to get to know one another intimately.
There are two great land barriers and one fairly extensive water barrier between the various parts of the country. Every rural constituency in that province with the exception of two, and one urban constituency, indicated that they endorsed the policies of the government and were behind the Minister of Agriculture. We must conclude that those are policies that the people of the west, particularly those of Saskatchewan, want.
The government headed by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) received a mandate from the people of Canada. The Prime Minister is to be congratulated because he did not look to any particular part of the country or any particular group of the people and say that he was going to further their particular interest. He looked at Canada as a whole. He realized that if Canada was to continue to play the part she has played in the past we must work together as a unit.
The western provinces, which are not so large in population or so well developed as those of central Canada, were inspired by that attitude. Instead of always wanting something more, they desire to pull their weight and add to the development of Canada rather than to continually criticize the government and complain that it is not doing enough for them.
The riches of the vast plains of western Canada can fulfil a destiny which is nationwide if not world-wide in its implications. It has been said in many quarters that the 45781-18

We have heard a good deal in this house about the over-production of wheat, but I think that if the world food situation is reviewed it will be found that there will be plenty of mouths to consume even the maximum food production of this country, provided the mechanics of international trade can be adjusted in order to permit that food to be sent where it is needed. I have every confidence that this government will in the future, as in the past, find means to distribute this food throughout the world, thereby doing a great service to humanity. We have just come through one terrible war and we abhor the thought of another. I believe students of international affairs will agree with me that people who are well fed and have room to live in and expand are hard to stir up to that point of dissatisfaction where they can be recruited into large armies of aggression.
As I have said before, western Canada has the space and is anxious to take its place in the development of the whole country. There is one important factor, however, which has to be taken into consideration before these vast spaces can be utilized to their fullest extent. To put it in simple words, the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta in the main have too small an annual rainfall to permit intensive cultivation in small acreages. While nature has not endowed the west with rainfall, she has endowed it with facilities so that man can create, and is creating, under the leadership of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), conditions whereby small acreages of land can be intensively farmed, thus making many homes for people who are still awaiting the day when they can leave their crowded mother country and come to this great dominion.
These conditions are provided by the water development projects that either have been completed or are under construction on the prairies at the present time. Some hon. members are fully aware of the increased production of various kinds of crops on small acreages which has been going on in Alberta for some time. These projects were started by private companies, but through experience it has been found that this type of development lends itself more to government than to private operation. Consequently the prairie farm rehabilitation organization has taken over most of the Alberta projects at the present time. There is a large area of ideal country in Saskatchewan which will lend

I think it is appropriate to acquaint hon. members of the house with the new constituency which I have the honour to represent. It came into being in 1947 by virtue of an act of parliament. The name is familiar to all hon. members. It was named after the late Cardinal Villeneuve, a prominent clergyman, a great Canadian, and a prince of the Catholic church, who went out of his way to preach Canadian unity. The new constituency is composed of the northern part of the old riding of Pontiac and includes the whole of the provincial riding of Rouyn-Noranda, part of the riding of Abitibi East, and part of Abitibi West. It is 100 miles in length and its greatest width is 60 miles. In it are to be found the following cities and towns: Rouyn, Noranda, Duparquet, Cadillac, Malartic, Val d'Or, Bourlamaque, Sullivan, and Perron. There are also numerous villages. When one hears those names one realizes that the riding of Villeneuve must have within its boundaries most of the gold and base metal mines of northwestern Quebec. Of twenty-four operating mines, twenty-two are in the constituency of Villeneuve. Twenty-five years ago, within the territory now included in that constituency, there were not more than 1,500 to 2,000 people. Today that area has a population of approximately 60,000. The main industries in my constituency are mining, agriculture and lumbering.
The speech from the throne deals with very important legislation which is to be enacted by this parliament, but it is not my intention to analyse that speech. The mover

and seconder of the address, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing), the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) and many other distinguished members have reviewed that legislation, and I only wish to say a few words about two or three items. No doubt you have guessed that I would like to say a few words on the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Since His Excellency opened the first session of the 21st parliament many countries, including Canada, have devalued their currencies. The Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Gibson) gave a statement concerning the continuation of aid under that emergency act, in which he said that the legislation would be amended at the end of the calendar year 1949 and would be abandoned at the end of 1950.
I want to point out to hon. members that the mining industry is very important and should not be permitted to decline; that nothing should be left undone to encourage the discovery of new mines. Prospecting has been on the decline for the last three years or so, owing to the fact that the real prospector, the artisan, the man who may discover a new mine, has not been able to go into the field because of lack of funds and also because of a lack of support on the part of the public. We hope that a revival of public interest will provide prospectors with the necessary money to continue their work and find new mines. I do not believe most people realize that base metal mines are found when the prospector is looking for gold mines. We do not know the exact reason for that, but it is a fact, especially in northwestern Quebec and I believe also in northern Ontario, that all the base metal mines have been found by prospectors looking for gold. We have a good example in the Noranda mine, which was found by a prospector looking for gold. Similarly the Waite Amulet mine, the Golden Manitou, and recently the East Sullivan mine, all were found when prospectors were looking for gold. So it is important that we encourage prospecting.
During the last two or three years many mines in process of development have had to close because of increased costs in wages and materials, and also because the price of their final product was too low. Most important of all, but for the aid given under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act many other producing mines would have been forced to close. Fortunately, however, our government came to their aid.

Immediately following mention of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in the speech from the throne we see, "Prairie Farm Assistance Act." I wish I might also find mention of a clay belt farm assistance act. I would not want to paint the position of our farmers in black, but I would like to explain to the best of my ability the situation that exists in my constituency and in others along the clay belt which extends from Senneterre in Quebec to Hearst in Ontario. In the riding of Villeneuve farming is a relatively new industry, having been established only some twenty-five years ago. Now many of our farmers are at a stage where they need help and guidance! They need help in connection with their livestock, and in connection with the classification, storage and distribution of their products. Studies of these various problems are now being made by local organizations, but it is only with the help of duly qualified technicians and financial aid from the government that a program of such breadth can be carried out. We have the markets. There are over forty thousand people in the cities and towns I have mentioned. Carloads of such commodities as meat, vegetables, dairy products and poultry come from outside the district and are distributed by many merchants in the different localities. In such a situation you would think the local products would find an outlet. I believe hon. members are aware of the fact, however, that a grocer cannot buy products that are not classified. If he is not assured of a steady flow of products from these farmers, he cannot buy from them.
Our farmers need a distribution centre in which they can find facilities such as slaughter houses, cold storage and good management for the distribution of their products. These facilities are lacking, so the flow of products is not steady. This is partly due to a lack of guidance in distribution. Further progress could be made by a livestock improvement program, jointly operated with a program for the development of grasses. This would enable the farmers of the district to continue the production of livestock on a sustained basis. This applies to other areas along the clay belt as well as to the grey wooded soils of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as another of the elected representatives of the new province of Newfoundland,
I trust you will think it not inappropriate if I crave the indulgence of the house while I say a few words on the occasion of my being admitted to the fellowship of this house. I say "fellowship" advisedly because of the warm reception I have received from all hon. members I have met since coming to Ottawa. I wish to thank them for the many kind offices that have been performed for me. I may say that I am quickly getting to feel that I am not a new member, but an old member. I wish to thank all those who have given me such a warm reception and to say that I feel the welcome to me is not only a personal welcome, but a welcome to Newfoundland as well.
May I be permitted to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your elevation to the high position you now hold? I should like also to congratulate the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert) and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing), the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Not making any

claims to being a speaker myself, I can well appreciate the eloquence and the delivery exhibited by these speakers in the excellent addresses they presented.
May I also place on the record my congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on the splendid victory which he achieved on June 27. I can assure him that the radio reports were enthusiastically received in Newfoundland.
I think it a thrilling and splendid thing that the dream of the fathers of confederation has at last been realized. Newfoundland is now a part of Canada and Newfoundlanders can join hands with the peoples of the other provinces from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Vancouver island as a united Canada, truly from ocean to ocean, and play their part with them as fellow Canadians.
During the war years when members of the Canadian forces were part of the visiting forces in Newfoundland, strong individual friendships were formed between men and women of the armed forces of Canada and Newfoundlanders wherever in that country those forces were stationed, and although some time has elapsed since then, these warm friendships still exist and will continue to do so and serve further to strengthen in a personal way the ties of our political and economic union. Yet another bond is that forged in war between the men and women of Newfoundland who served side by side with Canadians in the armed forces of Canada.
At this time, perhaps I may be permitted to say something of the facts which led up to the union of Newfoundland with Canada. As all hon. members no doubt know, before the union with Canada Newfoundland was governed by a form of government known as a commission of government. This government took office in 1934 when the letters patent of Newfoundland were suspended by act of the United Kingdom parliament and a commission of government was set up under new letters patent. It was never contemplated that commission of government should be a permanent form of government in Newfoundland. On or about December 11, 1945, Prime Minister Attlee announced that, to enable the people of the island to come to a free and informed decision as to their future form of government, a national convention would be elected to inquire into the financial and economic position of the island and to make recommendations to His Majesty's government with regard to possible future forms of government for submission to the people in a national referendum. Accordingly in 1946 the national convention was set up in Newfoundland. The act setting up the

national convention was Act No. 16 of 1946. Section 3 of that act reads:
It shall be the duty and function of the convention to consider and discuss among themselves as elected representatives of the people of Newfoundland the changes that have taken place in the financial and economic situation of the island since 1934, and, bearing in mind the extent to which the high revenues of recent years have been due to wartime conditions, to examine the position of the country and to make recommendations to His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom as to possible forms of future government to be put before the people at a national referendum.
The national convention was then set up and its deliberations began. During the course of those deliberations a delegation was sent to Ottawa to discuss the possible terms of confederation.
